content: The national guidelines for the management and control of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) have undergone revisions to incorporate new evidence and improve clinical outcomes. These updates include detailed methodologies for guideline development, focusing on the treatment of genital herpes simplex virus (HSV) infections. Below is a breakdown of the key points and recommendations: Priority Setting and Survey Analysis Four priority STI surveys were conducted, achieving a 90–100% response rate from STI subgroup members. The surveys analyzed populations, interventions, and outcomes. Outcomes were categorized based on their average rating: critical (7–9), important (4–6), and not important (1–3). Only critical and important outcomes were included in the guidelines. Questions scoring less than 7 were retained for consistency, and comparisons were limited to critical interventions and their comparison with important interventions. First Clinical Episode of Genital HSV Infection Question 1: Should the first clinical episode of genital HSV infection be treated? Question 2: How should the first clinical episode of genital HSV infection be treated? Recommended treatments include: Acyclovir 200 mg orally five times daily for 5–10 days. Acyclovir 400 mg orally three times daily for 5–10 days. Valacyclovir 500 mg–1 g orally twice daily for 5–10 days. Famciclovir 250 mg orally three times daily for 5–10 days. Critical outcomes include the duration of the clinical episode, HSV severity/pain, and quality of life. Important outcomes include ulcer healing, side effects, HSV transmission, shedding duration, HIV transmission/acquisition, and compliance. For pregnant women, additional critical outcomes include maternal outcomes (e.g., cesarean section) and fetal outcomes (e.g., neonatal herpes, teratogenicity, fetal loss, toxicity, neonatal death). Recurrent Clinical Episodes of Genital HSV Infection Episodic Therapy (Questions 3 and 4): Should recurrent (not frequent) genital HSV infections be treated with episodic therapy? How should recurrent (not frequent) genital HSV infections be treated with episodic therapy? Recommended episodic treatments include: Acyclovir 200 mg orally five times daily for 5 days. Acyclovir 400 mg orally three times daily for 3–5 days. Acyclovir 800 mg orally twice daily for 5 days or three times daily for 2 days. Valacyclovir 500 mg orally twice daily for 3–5 days or 1 g orally twice daily for 3–5 days. Famciclovir 125 mg orally twice daily for 5 days or 1 g orally twice daily for 1 day. Suppressive Therapy (Questions 5 and 6): Should recurrent, frequent genital HSV infections be treated with suppressive or episodic therapy? How should recurrent, frequent genital HSV infections be treated with suppressive therapy? Recommended suppressive treatments include: Acyclovir 200 mg orally four times daily or 400 mg orally twice daily. Valacyclovir 500 mg or 1 g orally once daily. Famciclovir 250 mg orally twice daily. Critical outcomes include recurrent clinical episodes, HSV severity/pain, quality of life, HSV transmission, and shedding. Important outcomes include side effects, HIV transmission/acquisition, HIV viral load, compliance, and ulcer healing. Severe Clinical Episodes of Genital or Anorectal HSV Infection Question 7: How should severe clinical episodes of genital or anorectal HSV infection be treated? Recommended treatments include: Acyclovir 400 mg orally 3–5 times daily. Acyclovir 5–10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours. Foscarnet 40 mg/kg IV every 8 hours. Cidofovir 5 mg/kg once weekly. Critical outcomes include the duration of the clinical episode, ulcer healing, HSV severity/pain, and quality of life. Important outcomes include side effects, HIV viral load, compliance, HSV transmission, shedding duration, and HIV transmission/acquisition. Evidence Review and Methodology Evidence was gathered using a hierarchical approach to avoid duplication of previously published reviews. Systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized studies were conducted when necessary. Search strategies were developed by information specialists using PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions and included keywords such as herpes, shingles, zoster, varicella, and HSV. No restrictions were placed on language, publication status, or study design. RCTs were prioritized for critical and important outcomes, while non-randomized studies were included when RCT evidence was unavailable. Patient Values, Preferences, and Feasibility Studies on patient values, preferences, acceptability, equity, and feasibility were identified through systematic searches. These studies included both quantitative and qualitative research methods. Patient preferences were assessed using tools such as questionnaires, scales, and focus group discussions. Outcomes included satisfaction, adherence, and attitudes toward treatment options. Cost Analysis The cost of treatment was calculated based on the market price of medications, dosage, and treatment duration. Additional costs, such as syringes or injection time, were not included. The final cost for a full course of treatment was determined by multiplying the number of doses per day by the number of treatment days, plus 25% of procurement costs. Guideline Development and Recommendations The Guideline Development Group (GDG) met in October 2015 to finalize recommendations. Evidence profiles and decision frameworks were presented, and interventions were evaluated using the GRADE approach. The GRADE criteria assessed the quality of evidence based on study design, risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, effect size, and other factors. Recommendations were made based on a population perspective, considering the balance of benefits and harms, patient values, and resource use. These guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for the effective management of genital HSV infections, ensuring improved patient outcomes and resource optimization.
